segments.title: Why Insect-class gunboats served in China and Mesopotamia
segments.summary: The Royal Navy built the Insect class for river campaigns and distant-station work, where shallow draft mattered more than cruiser speed or armor.
segments.body: The class belonged to river and station warfare, despite six-inch guns that superficially resembled light-cruiser armament. The related Fly-class boats were built for the Tigris and Mesopotamia campaigns, where rivers carried supplies and firepower. Their design also drew on earlier river operations along the Nile and on lessons from the American Civil War. In China, the same shallow draft let gunboats carry an armed naval presence far inland. Firefly's Ottoman capture and recapture by Tarantula shows how directly these small craft could enter contested river operations.

evidence.note: The transcript calls the Insect class the large China gunboats and places the Fly class beside them as small China or Tigris gunboats.
The transcript ties the ships to the Tigris and Mesopotamia campaigns, river movement of goods, and gunboat presence in China.

segments.title: Why treaties barely constrained Insect-class gunboats
segments.summary: At under 2,000 tons, below 20 knots, and without torpedoes, the class sat in the treaty-era small-ship category despite its six-inch guns.
segments.body: Small gunboats sat outside the headline treaty limits. Their displacement, speed, and lack of torpedoes put them alongside sloops even though their six-inch guns gave them considerable local firepower. They carried no official armor, but crews could add improvised protection when the hull would bear the weight. Wartime refits introduced pom-poms, three-inch anti-aircraft guns, and 20 mm weapons. In 1939 Aphis and Ladybird exchanged their Mark VII six-inch guns for longer Mark XIII weapons removed from HMS Agincourt. Shallow draft opened rivers and close coastal waters to them, while poor seakeeping kept them out of rough seas.

evidence.note: The transcript says gunboats fit with sloops because they are under 2,000 tons, below 20 knots, and carry no torpedoes.
The transcript describes wartime weapon changes, lack of armor, improvised protection, and the 1939 transfer of HMS Agincourt's Mark XIII guns to Aphis and Ladybird.
The transcript describes distant-station presence, close-inshore access, and the ships being unsuitable for rough seas.

segments.title: Basra, Kuwait, and the Baghdad Railway in 1914
segments.summary: The opening Mesopotamia campaign connected the Basra landing, British protection of Kuwait, and an effort to block Ottoman and German reinforcement toward the Persian Gulf.
segments.body: The British Indian Expeditionary Force landed near Basra with the 6th Poona Division under Lieutenant-General Arthur Barrett and Sir Percy Cox as political officer. Sheikh Mubarak Al Sabah of Kuwait also sent forces against Ottoman positions near Umm Qasr and Basra. Britain then recognized Kuwait as an independent government under British protection. The operation interrupted completion of the Baghdad Railway and restricted Ottoman and German reinforcement toward the Persian Gulf. The advance stalled after Basra when the force turned north toward Baghdad, creating the operational problem that river gunboats would help solve.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies the 6th Poona Division, Lieutenant-General Arthur Barrett, Sir Percy Cox, Sheikh Mubarak Al Sabah, and Britain's recognition of Kuwait under British protection.
The transcript links the opening campaign to the Baghdad Railway, Persian Gulf reinforcement routes, the capture of Basra, and the difficulty of advancing north.

segments.title: Gunboats carry mobile fire support toward Kut and Baghdad
segments.summary: Insect and Fly-class gunboats made the advance from Basra toward Kut and Baghdad more practical by moving heavy firepower with the front.
segments.body: Once the campaign pushed north from Basra, land artillery had to be towed, emplaced, and prepared before firing. Insect and Fly-class gunboats could instead move with the advance and engage from the river. Their fire while under way was imperfect, but forts and shore batteries were usually stationary targets. This combination of mobility and six-inch firepower made the river flotilla central to the advance toward Kut and Baghdad.

evidence.note: The transcript says the Insect and Fly-class gunboats supported river movement and that advances depended on their mobile fire support.
The transcript summarizes their fire-support purpose and caveats their accuracy while moving.

segments.title: HMS Aphis from the Danube to Mediterranean fire support
segments.summary: HMS Aphis carried a First World War river-gunboat design from the Danube and China Station into Second World War fire support across the Mediterranean.
segments.body: Built by Ailsa Shipbuilding, HMS Aphis served on the Danube in 1917 before spending much of her career on the China Station. Her Second World War battle honours covered the Mediterranean from Libya and Sicily to the Adriatic and southern France. That record shows how a specialist river craft could be reassigned to coastal bombardment and inshore support far from its original theatre. The hull's usefulness lasted across two wars because sheltered-water duties still matched its shallow draft and heavy guns.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies Aphis's builder, Danube service in 1917, and long China Station career.
The transcript lists Aphis's Second World War honours in Libya, Sicily, the Adriatic, and southern France.

segments.title: HMS Bee and the cost of one-for-one replacement
segments.summary: HMS Bee was scrapped after HMS Scorpion replaced her, leaving no reserve when the newer gunboat was lost to Japanese surface forces.
segments.body: HMS Bee was sold for scrap at Shanghai in March 1939 after HMS Scorpion replaced her. Scorpion belonged to the newer Dragonfly class, but Japanese cruiser and destroyer forces sank her in February 1942. The case is explicitly framed with hindsight: bringing Bee home would have preserved another useful inshore hull. One-for-one replacement reduced resilience because the discarded predecessor could no longer cover the loss of the new ship.

evidence.note: The transcript says Bee was sold for scrap in Shanghai after replacement by the newly built gunboat HMS Scorpion.
The transcript identifies Scorpion's loss to Japanese cruiser and destroyer forces in February 1942.
The transcript gives Bee's March 1939 sale and argues that returning her home would have been useful, while marking the judgment as hindsight.

segments.title: HMS Cockchafer confronts the Wanhsien seizures
segments.summary: The opening phase of the 1926 Wanhsien incident shows HMS Cockchafer using armed presence to reverse seizures of British merchant ships.
segments.body: The 1926 Wanhsien incident began when troops under General Yang Sen seized the British merchant ship SS Wanhsien. HMS Cockchafer's nearby six-inch guns gave her boarding party coercive leverage, and the soldiers released the vessel after a heated confrontation. A later collision involving SS Wanliu killed Chinese soldiers and prompted another attempted ship seizure, which Cockchafer also interrupted. River gunboats protected commercial access and diplomatic claims, but local power struggles, demands on trading companies, and accidental violence could turn a presence mission into a crisis.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces HMS Cockchafer in the 1926 Wanhsien incident and describes the seizure of a British merchant ship and the gunboat-backed intervention.
The transcript discusses the seizure campaign as a possible effort by General Yang to extract more resources from Western trading companies.
The transcript describes the Wanliu collision, loss of Chinese soldiers and materiel, and Cockchafer's intervention against another attempted seizure.

segments.title: Wanhsien rescue attempt becomes a firefight
segments.summary: A camouflaged merchant ship, naval boarding party, and covering gunboats turn the Wanhsien hostage rescue into a costly river battle.
segments.body: After General Yang's forces captured British officers and concentrated artillery ashore, negotiations failed and the Royal Navy attempted a forced rescue. The British camouflaged and armored SS Kiawo, then crewed her with sailors from Cockchafer, Despatch, Scarab, Mantis, and other gunboats. The boarding party recovered the hostages under fire while Widgeon and Cockchafer exchanged fire with Chinese troops and lost officers before withdrawing. The hostages were saved, but the merchant ships remained behind, Chinese soldiers and civilians were killed, property was destroyed, and coercive presence had become open combat.

evidence.note: The transcript describes General Yang's escalation, failed negotiations, and the Royal Navy's conversion and manning of SS Kiawo for the rescue attempt.
The transcript follows Kiawo's approach, the boarding under fire, hostage recovery, covering gunfire, British casualties, and withdrawal.
The transcript frames the action as the moment gunboat diplomacy's bluff was called and describes the destructive aftermath and pressure on General Yang.

segments.title: HMS Cricket's air attack, write-off, and wreck off Cyprus
segments.summary: HMS Cricket moved from China to Mediterranean inshore duty before an Italian air attack left a wreck that still survives off Cyprus.
segments.body: HMS Cricket served in Mesopotamia and the Russian Civil War before joining the China Station. Transferred to the Mediterranean Inshore Squadron in 1940, she was crippled by Italian aircraft in 1941. The Royal Navy declared her a constructive total loss and stripped her for spares. Her hulk later became an RAF target off Cyprus, where the wreck remains accessible to divers. The career shows both the utility and the air vulnerability of an old shallow-draft gunboat.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Cricket's transfer from China to the Mediterranean, her crippling by Italian air attack, and her declaration as a constructive total loss.
The transcript says Cricket's hulk was towed to Cyprus, used for RAF target training, and remains accessible to divers.

segments.title: The Panay incident as a Yangtze flashpoint
segments.summary: Attacks on USS Panay, Ladybird, and Bee show how river patrols, rescue work, press access, and diplomacy collided during the war in China.
segments.body: During the Second Sino-Japanese War, British and American gunboats worked the same crowded stretch of the Yangtze. Ladybird and Bee were attacked, reached the scene, and helped collect survivors from USS Panay. Aircraft also strafed small boats carrying wounded people despite large US flags painted on Panay. Times correspondent Colin MacDonald was aboard, while newsreel cameramen Norman Alley and Eric Mayell recorded the attack. Foreign gunboats offered reporters a way to reach the fighting with some protection, which also made any attack harder to contain or obscure. These vessels could serve as patrol craft, rescue platforms, diplomatic signals, press access, and flashpoints at the same time.

evidence.note: The transcript says Ladybird and Bee were also attacked, reached the scene to pick up survivors, and that Japan accepted responsibility and apologized.
The transcript describes the attack on USS Panay, machine-gunning of small boats, and the American flag painted on the ship.
The transcript explains why journalists and other observers used American or British gunboats to get close to fighting while retaining some protection.

segments.title: HMS Tarantula becomes a support ship and fleet flagship
segments.summary: HMS Tarantula's conversion from river combatant to repair and office ship culminated in service as Admiral Bruce Fraser's early British Pacific Fleet flagship.
segments.body: HMS Tarantula recaptured Firefly from the Ottoman Empire and supported fighting on the route to Baghdad during the First World War. By the Second World War she had become a repair, support, and office ship at Trincomalee. That unglamorous capacity made her useful to Admiral Bruce Fraser, who used her as his British Pacific Fleet flagship in 1944 before larger headquarters space was available. The conversion released frontline warships from static command and support duties. In May 1946 the Royal Navy sank Tarantula as a gunnery target in the Bay of Bengal.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Tarantula in repair, support, and office service and says Admiral Bruce Fraser used her as his British Pacific Fleet flagship in 1944.
The transcript contrasts Tarantula's earlier river combat with her later flagship form and notes her sinking as a gunnery target in 1946.

segments.title: HMS Moth is scuttled, recovered, and lost in Japanese service
segments.summary: HMS Moth's recovery after the fall of Singapore shows how denying a damaged vessel could fail and return a gunboat to war under a new flag.
segments.body: HMS Moth was under repair when Singapore fell, and the British scuttled her to prevent capture. Japanese forces nevertheless recovered the gunboat and returned her to service as Suma. She survived until March 1945, when a mine sank her with the loss of eight crewmen. The sequence makes scuttling a concrete wartime logistics problem: a wreck was only denied to the enemy if damage, time, and local salvage capacity made recovery impractical.

evidence.note: The transcript says Moth was under repair at Singapore, was scuttled when the city fell, and was then recovered by Japan.
The transcript says the recovered gunboat struck a mine in March 1945 and sank with eight crewmen lost.

segments.title: HMS Ladybird supports Bardia, Kastellorizo, and Tobruk
segments.summary: Ladybird's Mediterranean service demonstrates the class's value in bombardment and amphibious support despite age, low speed, and air vulnerability.
segments.body: HMS Ladybird had to be stripped and towed from Singapore toward the Mediterranean because the old shallow-draft hull was poorly suited to an ocean crossing. Damage during the journey limited her to seven knots, yet she bombarded Bardia during Operation Compass and landed Royal Marines on Kastellorizo during Operation Abstention. She later supported Tobruk by shelling Gazala airfield and ferrying supplies until dive bombers set her on fire in shallow water. The wreck remained above the surface, so her three-inch gun continued serving as an anti-aircraft weapon.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Ladybird's stripped-down tow from Singapore, hull damage, seven-knot limit, and resulting Port Said guard duty.
The transcript covers bombardment of Bardia, the Kastellorizo landing, Tobruk support, and Ladybird's crippling by dive bombers.
The transcript says Ladybird's three-inch gun continued in use as an anti-aircraft weapon because the wreck remained above water.

segments.title: HMS Gnat at Nanking and the next gunboat generation
segments.summary: HMS Gnat's Nanking service and relief by HMS Grasshopper connect interwar protection duties with the Royal Navy's newer Dragonfly-class gunboats.
segments.body: HMS Gnat helped protect British and other international civilians during the Nanking incident. From 1936 she also carried Judy, a liver-and-white pointer, as the ship's dog. Her relief by HMS Grasshopper introduced the Dragonfly class, showing that the Royal Navy still wanted purpose-built river gunboats late in the 1930s. The six newer boats carried four-inch guns and continued the same close-water presence mission with a more modern design. Gnat therefore links the Insect class's station work to the next generation of British river craft.

evidence.note: The transcript says Gnat participated in the Nanking incident and helped protect British and other international citizens in China.
The transcript identifies Judy, a liver-and-white pointer, as Gnat's ship's dog from 1936.
The transcript says Gnat was relieved by HMS Grasshopper and identifies the six newer Dragonfly-class gunboats and their four-inch armament.

segments.title: HMS Gnat survives a U-79 torpedo off Tobruk
segments.summary: Gnat's survival after a U-79 torpedo hit illustrates both the durability and the adaptable afterlife of an old inshore gunboat.
segments.body: HMS Gnat joined destroyers and the monitor Terror in supporting the 6th Australian Division's assault into Tobruk. U-79 torpedoed her in October 1941, but the small gunboat remained afloat and was towed to Alexandria. Although declared a constructive total loss, she served for four years as a fixed anti-aircraft platform before scrapping in 1945. The class's shallow draft let its six-inch guns move close to landing areas and fire accurately against shore targets. Gnat's survival preserved useful defensive firepower from a hull that could no longer operate at sea.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Gnat's support for the Australian assault into Tobruk, her torpedoing by U-79, tow to Alexandria, and constructive total loss.
The transcript emphasizes Gnat's subsequent fixed anti-aircraft service and the surprising survival of the torpedo hit.
The transcript summarizes the class's close-inshore fire-support value during troop landings.

segments.title: Scrapped Insect-class hulls and the late Dragonfly program
segments.summary: Prewar disposal of Insect-class hulls and late construction of the Dragonfly class left Britain with little margin when several newer gunboats were lost.
segments.body: HMS Mantis was sold in January 1940, while Glowworm had gone in 1928 and Bee in 1939. The timing mattered because treaty rules left Britain free to build more small gunboats, yet most of the Dragonfly class was not laid down until 1937 or 1938. Bee was cancelled in March 1940, Mosquito was lost off Dunkirk that June, and Dragonfly, Grasshopper, and Scorpion were all lost in February 1942. Locust alone survived the war among the completed boats listed here. The sequence supports a narrow procurement judgment: specialist inshore vessels could have been built earlier and in greater depth without consuming treaty-limited capital-ship tonnage.

evidence.note: The transcript lists the disposal of Mantis, Glowworm, and Bee, then argues that treaty rules still allowed gunboats and sloops to be built in useful numbers.
The transcript gives the late Dragonfly-class construction dates, Bee's cancellation, the losses of Mosquito, Dragonfly, Grasshopper, and Scorpion, and Locust's survival.

segments.title: Gunboats and sloops as force multipliers
segments.summary: A steady peacetime program for small combatants could have covered river, inshore, anti-submarine, and escort work while preserving destroyers for the fleet.
segments.body: Interwar defence debates concentrated on carriers, battleships, cruisers, and raw destroyer numbers, leaving small combatants largely unexamined. Emergency wartime construction then produced cheap, basic ships when a steady peacetime program could have refined gunboats and sloops year by year. A suggested program of a pair of roughly 700-ton gunboats annually would have been treaty-safe and could have sustained China Station, river, and inshore roles. Sloops could take anti-submarine and convoy escort work, while gunboats handled rivers and landing support. Each small ship released a destroyer for fleet duty. Even older V and W-class destroyers retained torpedoes and speed, so freeing them increased the number of fleet combatants available alongside newer H, Tribal, and J classes.

evidence.note: The transcript criticizes interwar attention to headline fleet units and contrasts emergency construction with a steady peacetime small-ship program.
The transcript proposes building a pair of roughly 700-ton gunboats each year and argues that treaty rules did not prevent such a program.
The transcript explains how sloops and gunboats could release older and newer destroyer classes for fleet work, making the small vessels force multipliers.
